articles.text: The City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) invite community members to a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Piedmont Community Pool at 11 a.m. this Saturday, December 17. Refreshments will be served. The event, which will take place behind the Recreation Department at the site of the former pool, will celebrate the City Council’s recent hiring of a contractor to build an aquatic facility at a cost of approximately $23,870,000. Construction of the new pool is expected to begin in early 2023, and the new pool could open as soon as spring 2024. City officials and PRFO leaders will be joined by pool users young and old to thank the many volunteers, community advocates, and generous donors who have worked tirelessly over the years to make this project a reality. Olympic swimmer Dana Vollmer will be on hand for greetings and photos with her five gold medals. “This is a very exciting time for aquatic lovers and the entire Piedmont community,” said Steve Collins, President of PRFO. “Holding an inclusive event really represents what this effort is about. Not just for the water aspect, the Pool facility is also a perfect destination for birthday parties, social events, team get-togethers and all other types of gatherings. It will be an essential part of Piedmonters’ lives for decades.” To date, PRFO has raised over $1 million towards a fundraising goal of $2.1 million to complete the community pool as designed. PRFO initiated a capital campaign in partnership with the City in August 2022 to bridge a funding gap created by a sharp rise in construction costs. This effort builds on the success of previous PRFO fundraising in support of Hampton Park and the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Primary funding for the pool replacement project comes from Measure UU, approved by Piedmont voters in November 2020. Measure UU authorized the sale of $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to fund a new community pool. The City of Piedmont, Piedmont City Council, and PRFO thank the many generous donors who have contributed to support the new pool, including the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Education Foundation, and remain grateful to the entire community for their ongoing support for this project. For more information on the new pool, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ newpool. To contribute to the capital campaign, visit prfo.org/ piedmont-community-pool.

articles.text: On a warm, sunny day about 10 years ago, I sat on the edge of the pool next to Betsy Andersen. I’ve known Betsy since she was a teenage lifeguard with our younger daughter. She said she was going to spearhead another attempt to build a new pool, after repeated prior attempts had failed. I wished her luck and said I’d support her every step of the way, but that to make it happen, we had to build a facility that worked for the whole community, and we had to get all the aquatics stakeholders on board pushing for that pool. I jokingly made her promise to get it done before I turned 80. The City hired a firm to help us come up with a conceptual design. Multiple community meetings were held and by the end of 2016 a conceptual design master plan was approved. A 2017 study showed that the plan was financially viable. A community survey in 2018 showed that just over 50% of the community would support a bond issue to fund the new pool, far below the 2/3 needed to pass it. In 2020, the political consultants said there was no way you could bridge the gap from 50% to 2/3 to pass a bond measure, but we did it anyway in the middle of a pandemic, when no one could meet or campaign door to door. Then, in 2021, the City hired ELS to design the actual pool facilities. They met with the community again to perfect the conceptual design, they told us the main pool in that design wouldn’t fit in the available space and came up with an alternative that would fit, one that everyone was even more excited about than the original design. In January, that design was approved, but two months later we were told the high construction inflation caused by the pandemic made it too expensive to build.
articles.title: New Pool getting closer, but we’re not there yet

articles.text: After receiving extensive feedback from residents affected by the prospective loss of parking spaces, the City has drafted a modified plan for bulb-outs on Oakland Avenue at the intersections of Jerome and El Cerrito Avenues. The city is now waiting for approval from AC Transit. When the initial bulb-out plan was approved by the City more than one year ago, on October 4, 2021, it was then presented to the public at an on-site meeting on November 1 last month. According to Piedmont Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, there was “pushback from many parties.” In addition to permanent bulb-outs — where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer — the plan provided for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. There was support for the four bulb-outs, but considerable opposition to a plan that would eliminate parking spaces by relocating of bus stops. As a result, they are working on new plans, with continual feedback from AC Transit. The new plan, said Gonzales, addresses a majority of the concerns of neighbors. Instead of a net loss of 10 parking spots, the newer revised plan would only involve three parking spaces, and in modified locations – one on El Cerrito Ave. in the downhill direction, and two at Jerome Avenue. “We were trying to figure out how much flexibility their [AC Transit’s] safety guidelines allowed for,” said Gonzales. “We found that we could keep the bus stops where they were. Ironically, there was enough space for the buses to pull in and out as a result of the curb changes presented by the bulb-outs. While the revised bulb-out plan is not yet finalized, it is currently under review by AC Transit. “We are optimistic about the results,” said Gonzales, “and most importantly about keeping the bus stops in their existing configuration. Now we’re just waiting for AC Transit to sign off.” After the new plan is finalized, Gonzales plans to hold a second informational public meeting about the bulb-outs to receive comments, questions, and other feedback from residents. Those with questions about the new bulb-out plan may send an e-mail to Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or call 420-3060.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has released an Initial Study and Negative Declaration for its proposed 6th Cycle Housing Element. The report is available for public review and comment through January 8. This is the next step in the City’s Housing Element update, a process that has been underway since Spring 2021. Part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by state and regional authorities. Adopting a Housing Element does not require these homes be built. Rather, the purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support the growth. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. A review of the City’s Draft Housing Element based on these guidelines determined that, as a policy document, the Housing Element alone will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. Physical changes that would result from the implementation of policies and programs proposed in the Housing Element are currently being studied as part of a programmatic Environmental Impact Report (EIR) covering updates to the City’s General Plan and changes to the City Code that would happen after the Housing Element is adopted. The Initial Study and Negative Declaration is available for download and review on the City’s website at the following link: https://bit.ly/3FDqFhg. Physical copies of the documents are available for review at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. Background The City submitted its proposed Draft Housing Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review on November 18, 2022. By Selen Ozturk After receiving extensive feedback from residents affected by the prospective loss of parking spaces, the City has drafted a modified plan for bulb-outs on Oakland Avenue at the intersections of Jerome and El Cerrito Avenues. The city is now waiting for approval from AC Transit. When the initial bulb-out plan was approved by the City more than one year ago, on October 4, 2021, it was then presented to the public at an on-site meeting on November 1 last month. According to Piedmont Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, there was “pushback from many parties.” In addition to permanent bulb-outs — where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer — the plan provided for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. There was support for the four bulb-outs, but considerable opposition to a plan that would eliminate parking spaces by relocating of bus stops. As a result, they are working on new plans, with continual feedback from AC Transit. The new plan, said Gonzales, addresses a majority of the concerns of neighbors. Instead of a net loss of 10 parking spots, the newer revised plan would only involve three parking spaces, and in modified locations – one on El Cerrito Ave. in the downhill direction, and two at Jerome Avenue. “We were trying to figure out how much flexibility their [AC Transit’s] safety guidelines allowed for,” said Gonzales. “We found that we could keep the bus stops where they were. Ironically, there was enough space for the buses to pull in and out as a result of the curb changes presented by the bulb-outs. While the revised bulb-out plan is not yet finalized, it is currently under review by AC Transit. “We are optimistic about the results,” said Gonzales, “and most importantly about keeping the bus stops in their existing configuration. Now we’re just waiting for AC Transit to sign off.” After the new plan is finalized, Gonzales plans to hold a second informational public meeting about the bulb-outs to receive comments, questions, and other feedback from residents. Those with questions about the new bulb-out plan may send an e-mail to Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or call 420-3060. Housing Element comments due January 8 By Selen Ozturk The City of Piedmont has released an Initial Study and Negative Declaration for its proposed 6th Cycle Housing Element. The report is available for public review and comment through January 8. This is the next step in the City’s Housing Element update, a process that has been underway since Spring 2021. Part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by state and regional authorities. Adopting a Housing Element does not require these homes be built. Rather, the purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support the growth. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. A review of the City’s Draft Housing Element based on these guidelines determined that, as a policy document, the Housing Element alone will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. Physical changes that would result from the implementation of policies and programs proposed in the Housing Element are currently being studied as part of a programmatic Environmental Impact Report (EIR) covering updates to the City’s General Plan and changes to the City Code that would happen after the Housing Element is adopted. The concert, which consists of the full choir and soloists accompanied by a full professional orchestra, is conducted by the church’s Music Director, Stephen Main. Stephen, winner of the John Ness Beck Award for Best American Choral Composition, is a well-known composer. Among his many accomplishments, he has composed scores for several movies and wrote the Centennial Fanfare for the City of Piedmont. The beautiful interior of the church, which was designed by Piedmont’s most prominent architect, Albert Farr, enhances the concert experience. Following the concert, audience members are invited to a gala reception in Guild Hall with hot and cold gourmet hors d’oeuvres served with wine and non-alcoholic punch. The concert, For All this Night, will reprise the very first concert of the series. The text for the music comes mainly from the 15th and 16th centuries, “one of the first of several golden ages in English carol-writing”, explained Dr. Main. “Carols were the music of common people rather than of liturgical professionals,” he said. “They offered an opportunity to flesh out the biblical stories, which by themselves are often quite spare in the details of Jesus’ birth. For example, in one of the movements of For All this Night, there is an imaginative dialogue between Mary and her newborn son.” Inspired by these Renaissance era carols, Main has composed fresh melodies for them. articles.text: Amal Smith will term out of office following the Piedmont School Board meeting tonight, December 14, after nearly nine years as a volunteer board member. Smith took some time to catch up with the Post about how the position and the school district has changed over time, the future of PUSD, what it was like to be President of the Board at a time when COVID changed everything. A 25-year resident of Piedmont, Smith won her seat on the school board in February 2014 as the top vote getter. In 2018 former teacher Megan Pillsbury, took the election by storm, and garnered the most votes from Piedmont residents. As an incumbent seeking reelection, Smith won over Julie Caskey by 47 votes. “I don’t like knocking on people’s doors because I don’t like people knocking on my door at the end of the day. [The strategy] worked,” Smith said about the 2018 campaign. Smith was at the helm of the Board when COVID hit, and the basic delivery method of education had to be rethought. For the last six years Smith has worked as Associate Dean for Financial Affairs at the UCSF School of Medicine. “There was this interesting synergy or alignment because what I learned daily at UCSF could help shape what I was thinking about what we needed to do as a school district,” she said. Smith oversaw the school board through some of the district’s toughest times. The school campuses closed and previously routine board meetings turned into six-hour marathons. Cory Smegal succeeded Smith as board president in December 2020. In thinking of her time on the board, Smith pointed to two areas in which she takes significant pride: board policy on sexual harassment, and the work done towards Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEI-B). “I think we’re moving in the right direction,” Smith said. “I want to not lose sight of this idea of social-emotional wellness; and hold that in the same place as we hold academic excellence. You cannot have lifelong learners if you don’t help kids feel they are in a place where they can learn.” “What I’m really interested in is how do we learn and get better at the things we need to get better at. I think our community is really wrestling with and actively working on [DEI-B] issues. I think we are headed in the direction of being more open and recognizing that experiences do vary,” Smith said. Smith acknowledged that the Amal Smith served on the school board from 2014-2022. relationship between the district and labor unions has been a bit rocky because of COVID. “But I think the basis of our relationships haven’t shifted. There’s deep respect for the work that gets done. I want us to continue to honor that; I don’t want us to ever be adversarial in a non-productive way,” she added. As for Smith’s own future, she is looking forward to having a shorter work day, but is wary of slowing down too much. “I have a plan of what I want to do when I retire, which is a few years down the road. Between now and then, I’ll be looking for some kind of opportunity to fill my time, because I’m happiest when I’m busy. And I’m happiest when I’m doing this kind of work,” Smith said. @REPBARBARALEE

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Pioneers, a First Tech Challenge robotics team. Piedmont Pioneers, a middle school First Tech Challenge robotics team, recently participated in a qualifying tournament in Saratoga. The team includes several team members from Piedmont. Their members are Aliya Vora, Dylan Wallway, Ed Balasingham, Elliott Briggs, Elsa Wallway, Grey Sanford, Max Carter and Sam Charslon. As one of the few all-middle school teams, the Pioneers competed on December 4 in Saratoga with mostly high schoolers. The competition format allows for multiple robot matches, which then lead to semifinals, then finals. There is also a presentation to the judges, where the teams discuss team strategy. In preparation for the tournament, the Pioneers ramped up practices to four times a week in order to get in more practice driving the robot and running through speeches, as well as making any last-minute coding or building adjustments. They woke up early Sunday morning to head to the event. After passing robot and field inspection with the tournament officials, they gathered with all competing teams to watch the opening ceremony. Then, the Pioneers completed the presentation, which consisted of speeches, a discussion of outreach events, engineering portfolio, and giving a run-through of the robot’s design. After finishing the interview, the team went back to watch the early robot matches and analyze other teams’ designs. After watching the first few rounds, the Pioneers stepped up to the field, robot in hand, ready for their first match. They started off strong in the autonomous period, but their alliance team’s robot malfunctioned and ended up barely losing the match for the Pioneers’ alliance. However, it was a good starting match, and allowed them to get in extra practice completing the tasks real-time on the field. During the next couple of matches, the team got used to the competition environment and started to hit their stride. With the help of their alliance partners, they managed to win three matches in a row. The last qualifying match started out well, but during the beginning of the match, the arm, a crucial component of the robot, broke. However, due to the help of their alliance partners, they were still able to win the round. The Pioneers ended up fourth overall for the robot game and were designated as an alliance captain. They chose two other teams that would be their alliance partners and competed in the elimination round as the third seed. The Pioneers were able to win two matches in a row, and with their alliance partners, continued on to the finals. After doing last minute checkups on all three robots, the two alliance teams competing in the finals were called to the stage. They set their robots down and the countdown began. The Pioneers’ alliance took off quickly and had a strong start, but the opposing alliances’ autonomous worked perfectly, allowing them to score a lot of points. In the driver-controlled period, they lost the match by a few points. The team won the Finalist Alliance Captain award, along with being named runner-up for the Motivate Award. Overall, the team learned a lot and now has knowledge it will use in its next competition on January 8.

At 1:07 p.m. on Monday, December 12, most students were racing down the steps for lunch at Piedmont Middle School. For 40 students, however, the lunch bell signaled the start of stiff competition in Ted Scherman’s classroom for Day One of the 2022 Spelling Bee. Only three of 40 students were eliminated in the first round of the week-long competition. Participation has increased in Scherman’s second year of hosting the event which normally draws an average of 20 participants. “Lots of kids signed up this year, possibly because there are fewer avenues available to compete academically,” said Scherman, a veteran 7th grade teacher. He plans on reviving the equally popular Geography Bee in the spring. It is no longer sponsored by National Geographic. “[The Spelling Bee] is a great way to test your smarts and it’s also super satisfying when you get a word correct,” said 8th grader Mira Sen, who finished third last year. Whizzed, cottonwood, slather, and M-U-R-A-L-S were all easily handled by the students. With little difficulty, 8th graders Eliza Berry and Emahn Sheikh spelled It was a packed and tense house for round one of the Spelling Bee in Ted Scherman’s class on Monday, as contestants easily outnumbered chairs. 8th grader Mira Sen finished in third place last year and has advanced to the 2nd round this year. out “joggled,” and “squinched” respectively. The school’s reigning champion, 8th grader Zoe Snyder, breezed into round two after confronted with “probably.” The three words that ousted some contestants were: “decide,” “orca,” and “constant.” “Spelling bees can be cruel and unusual; you can make one mistake and you are out,” warned Scherman at the start of the first day of competition. Last year’s Spelling Bee went for 14 rounds in six days of lunchtime competition before declaring a champion. This year, the winner of Piedmont’s Spelling Bee will be invited to an online test to qualify for the San Ramon Valley Rotary Regional Spelling Bee in March.

articles.text: Highlanders blank Bishop O’Dowd, Alameda 1-0 Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team opened its league season in strong fashion, defeating two local rivals, both by scores of 1-0. It posted a shutout of Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, December 7 in a road game, and produced the same result against the Alameda Hornets in front of their fans at Witter Field on Monday, December 12. “They are always tough teams to break down. Even when 1-nil down they sat and defended and made themselves difficult to beat,” said PHS coach Dan Chubbock. “Both teams were really just looking for that one chance and we didn’t give it to them.” Against Alameda, the Highlanders kept a high press and rarely let the Hornets out of their own defensive half. Alameda relied on long balls down the wings and trying to earn corner opportunities. But they finished without any shots on target and only a few shot attempts. Piedmont looked like the superior side in both victories, but a one-goal advantage never leaves players and coaches with any sense of security. They know that the results can change in a flash. “One goal never feels like it’s enough, so I did feel a little anxious that they needed just one chance to change the game. We controlled possession and controlled the chances. We looked in control, but we only scored one goal,” said Chubbock. “1-0 isn’t ideal but we were able to keep it out of our half and prevent them from creating chances. I think defensively, we’ve done well. I think there are some things we can do better offensively,” added senior Audrey Lam, who made an appearance during the summer with the U.S. Under-17 Women’s National team. Piedmont scored its lone goal against Alameda when freshman Miranda Liu sent a pass through to Lam for an easy one-on-one goal against the Hornets’ keeper. Liu also scored the game-winner against Bishop O’Dowd in the second half. Liu has been the starting striker in Chubbock’s attack, making a clear impact with the team. She scored and had an assist in Piedmont’s 3-2 loss to Miramonte in the season-opener on November 28. “It’s a great community. Everyone is really supportive, I knew some freshmen on varsity, and they really want to help me fit in,” said Liu. 1-0 win vs. Alameda Piedmont’s game-winner came in the 20th minute on a nice holdup play by Liu with two defenders on her, flicking a through pass to Lam all alone a few yards in front of the keeper. The Highlanders had several more chances to score in the first half and also had opportunities in the second half. After the goal, Emily Fitzgerald and Lam had shots on target in the 25th and 26th minutes that led to corner kicks. Michaela Bini also had a shot on target in the 28th minute and nearly scored in the 30th minute after Liu made a turn around a defender to find Bini, but her shot went wide as the keeper rushed out to make the block. In the second half, Piedmont continued the pressure to force turnovers in Alameda’s half. Staff Photos Audrey Lam scored against Alameda in the first half of Monday’s game. articles.text: Highlanders beat Archbishop Mitty by 4 points in final For just the second time in its 12-year history, Piedmont High has won its own Paris Twins Classic invitational tournament after narrowly beating Archbishop Mitty of San Jose 60-56 on Saturday, December 10. The tournament is named for twins Courtney and Ashley Paris, who led Piedmont to consecutive State championships in 2004 and 2005. Mitty received the SportsStar Magazine’s preseason No. 1 ranking in Northern California. Cardinal Newman of Santa Rosa, who PHS beat 66-34 on Friday, is ranked No. 17. This year’s Piedmont team is ranked No. 5 in Northern California. “It feels amazing just for us to win our own tournament. We haven’t gotten to match up against Mitty and we’ve always wanted to play them. For us to win means a lot. It feels like we’re a main target right now; it’s a lot of pressure but we’re ready to take it on,” said senior and team captain Trinity Zamora, who recently committed to play at San Diego State next year. Natalia Martinez led against Mitty with 20 points. Junior guard Natalia Martinez notably has already scored more than 1,000 points in less than three seasons. Making a debut on the team this year are transfer students Eva Levingston and Perseas Gioukaris. Their additions have allowed the Highlanders to have their most fluid offense in several years. ”It’s my comeback season and this feels like a year for our team to have a lot of success,” said Levingston. Championship game vs. Mitty Piedmont trailed Mitty 11-10 to end the first quarter but scored 20 points to take a 30-24 lead by halftime. PHS kept a five-point advantage going into the fourth quarter and closed out with a 4-point victory, 60-56. Mitty was playing without two of SportsStar Magazine’s preseason All-NorCal honorees, Morgan Cheli and Elana Weisman. Martinez started Piedmont’s scoring rally in the second quarter for an 18-13 lead, but Mitty scored six straight to regain the lead 19-18. The two sides traded the lead until PHS led 23-21 following a 3-pointer by Adrienne Blackwell. The Highlanders then scored seven of the next 10 points for a 30-24 lead at the break. Mitty narrowed Piedmont’s lead to 40-39 in the third period. With the score at 42-40, Maddie Hill knocked down a 3-pointer on an assist by Gioukaris. PHS and Mitty traded points until Piedmont took a 59-56 lead. In the final minute and after a series of fouls, Zamora hit one of two free throws for the 60-56 final. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team took a 1-nil loss to Berkeley at Witter Field on Wednesday, December 7. The Yellowjackets scored the game’ only goal in the ninth minute on a penalty kick. Ironically, Piedmont controlled the action and allowed Berkeley no clear looks on goal. “The [players] followed our game plan really well, Berkeley capitalized the one time we got caught out of position. After that moment, I’d argue we were the better team. We created the better opportunities to score another goal. We just can’t seem to get it over the line against Berkeley,” said coach Todd Sullivan. Looking like the better side against Berkeley, the defending WACC Foothill Division champions, is an encouraging sign for Piedmont as it begins competing in the league’s upper division. “My message to the team is to keep playing how they are. I’d argue that Berkeley is one of the best teams in our league and we’re competing with the best teams in a new league. It bodes well for the rest of the season,” said Sullivan. Piedmont finished the night with nine shots but just one on target, while Berkeley’s only shot on target was the penalty kick goal. Among the Highlanders’ strong points through three games has been their work from set pieces, and despite accumulating seven free kicks, they had no corners on the night. “We like the set plays. We’re very big, strong, and committed when in the air. It’s just a case of whether we can make something happen. We didn’t have any corners, but we were a threat on our set plays,” said Sullivan. The Highlanders had the first look of the night with a free kick in the first minute of action, resulting in a shot on target from distance. Berkeley drew the penalty kick on a long ball from midfield into the PHS penalty area, resulting in a Piedmont defender making contact with the Yellowjackets’ forward. Following the goal, Piedmont’s Sam Shelby had a shot trail wide in the 17th minute. Midfielder William Daniel also had shot attempts go over the net and wide of the mark in the 33rd and 38th minutes. articles.text: This treasure of California is among the best wintertime hikes in the Sierra Nevada. Donner Pass, an abandoned railway that was originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. The trek takes you through hollowed out mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass above Donner Lake. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the Donner Party tragically met their fate in the fierce winter of 1846— becoming the namesake of the lake and surrounding state park. The walk through the train tunnels is brief at just 2.1 miles to the final snow shed, but it gives you the magic of the Tahoe winter without being knee deep in snow. It’s a great place for children, families, or beginning snowshoers. During the warmer weather, you can walk past the last snow shed and continue to Donner Peak. From our starting point, we took the same route as our 2018 summer visit from McGlashan Point over a Native American petroglyph site that can be seen in warmer months. For now, it’s a popular sledding site with fresh snow. The Central Pacific Railroad created its route through Donner Pass in the spring of 1868 after a near three-year construction effort, accomplished Staff Photos A view of Donner Lake and the Donner Pass snow sheds appropriately covered in snow. China Wall is a platform created by Chinese workers to create the Central Pacific Railroad in 1868. through the efforts of Chinese railroad workers. The Donner Pass trail’s starting point, the China Wall, is a handmade construction that was the platform for the railroad leading into the starting tunnel. Inside the 1,659 foot Tunnel #6, hikers can spot a second Chinese Wall with boulders piled neatly up to the roof. A frozen wall of ice creates a surreal sight inside a snowshed. The entire walk has graffiti-covered walls inside the snow sheds. Some are distinctly graffiti art, such as the one on the right. Through the hollowed out mountains, some large icicles glisten through the tiny peaks of light along the roof and walls. Even some large frozen sections of water created massive blocks of ice that are clear as a piece of glass. You’ll find few sites that combine history and artwork with graffiti covering each wall of the sheds — some pieces magnificent in detail. Peeking around unsuspecting corners and behind walls, walkers with keen eyes can find some of California’s most prominent urban artists and large murals. Proper hiking gear is required in some ice-covered areas to prevent slipping and falls. With limited parking at the entrance lot to the tunnels, some may have to park n the sside of Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook. In our five miles of hiking, we passed just 27 hikers. Another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the China Wall. To access this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook on their GPS devices for common starting areas. Remember to return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and fr a hike to Donner Peak. Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on January 27, 2021.

articles.text: The Argentines have pushed their way to the 2022 World Cup Final on Sunday, December 18, after defeating Croatia 3-nil yesterday, December 13. They now await today’s result between France and Morocco. How amazing has this World Cup been? In last week’s Post, I wrote that Brazil and France were looking like the favorites, but that was until Croatia powered past the Canaries in penalty kicks. Morocco, meanwhile, has made magic as this year’s Cinderella story, defeating Portugal 1-0 in the quarterfinals. In next week’s Post, we’ll recap the tournament and all of the amazing moments from this Kylian Mbappe and France are the clear favorite walking into Wednesday’s semifinal. year’s games. Until then, here’s looking into tomorrow’s semifinal between France and Morocco, and the prospective final with Argentina. No. 4 France vs. No. 22 Morocco If you can tell by this writer’s last name, I’m going for France and will be wearing my Les Bleus jersey on Wednesday – and hopefully on Sunday as well. But, that being said, Morocco has been an absolute fairy tale of a story throughout this year’s World Cup, so all projections, market values, and rankings go completely out the window. The Moroccans ascent to the semifinals has been the stuff of legend. They won Group F over Croatia, helped send No. 2 ranked Belgium home in the group stage by defeating them 2-nil, defeated Spain in penalty kicks in the Round of 16, and were in control of No. 9 Portugal in last Saturday’s quarterfinals with a 1-0 win. Morocco is the first country from the African continent to reach the semifinals. France, meanwhile, is exactly where they were expected to be. They dwarf Morocco’s market value of €241.10 million by nearly €700 million with Les Bleus’ roster being valued at €937 million. Kylian Mbappe is tied for the Golden Boot race with Lionel Messi with five goals, and France is coming off of a big 2-1 win over England to qualify for the semi-finals. So who are the players to watch? With France, their team is ripe from top-to-bottom. Attacker Antoine Griezmann and wingers Ousmane Dembélé and Mbappe, striker Olivier Giroud, midfielder Aurélien Tchouaméni, and keeper Hugo Lloris have all been in stellar form. On Morocco, winger/midfielder Hakim Ziyech is always a threat, especially from set pieces. If Morocco can gain a free kick in a good area, watch out for Ziyech to whip in a shot. Striker Youssef En-Nesyri is another player to watch after scoring the Morocco pulled off yet another stunning upset when defeating Portugal 1-0. Can they make more magic in Wednesday’s semifinal against France? eventual game-winner against Portugal, while fullback Achraf Hakimi is one of the best players in the world at his position. If the Moroccan’s can pull off another upset, it will likely be because of strong defense. If France has an Achilles heel, it will be their back line. France got lucky when Harry Kane missed his penalty kick late in the second half of the quarterfinals, a shot that would have forced overtime. Theo Hernandez looked bad barreling into England’s Mason Mount to create a penalty kick situation. Perhaps Morocco can target France’s back line with long balls to force a similar error. I’m going with a 2-1 France win; Morocco makes things interesting, but France’s powerful attack controls the action. No. 3 Argentina in the Final Can the Messi Magic keep going? Argentina entered the tournament as a favorite to win and have proven that playing ugly sometimes gets the job done. It hasn’t been a perfect display from the Argentines after nearly taking an exit in the group stage. Its 2-1 win over Australia in the Round of 16 was unconvincing, it went to penalty kicks with Netherlands after a 2-2 draw before prevailing 4-3 on PKs. Argentina versus France was a clear favorite to occur in the pre-tournament predictions. I had it penciled in as my guess until watching Argentina lose to Saudi Arabia to open the group stage. It’s worth mentioning that Spain in 2010 was the last team to win the World Cup after dropping its opening group stage match. Both France and Argentina have an edge in several categories; France’s striker Giroud looks like a larger X-Factor than Julián Álvarez. Argentina’s back line with Christian Romero, Nicolás Otamendi, and Lisandro Martínez also has made its errors, but is clearly more physical than France’s defense. Messi is always a difference maker leading the attack and playing in the midfield compared to France’s Tchouaméni and Adrien Rabiot. Mbappe, meanwhile, is proving to be the world’s next all-time great player. You simply can’t match him with only one player. Argentina fans are undoubtedly hoping that Morocco makes the finals and would be the clear favorites if things fall that way – it’d be hard to not see Messi lifting the World Cup trophy. Again, defense gets the job done for Morocco, and if they can force penalty kicks anything could happen. Lionel Messi and Argentina await France or Morocco in Sunday’s finals.

But, that being said, Morocco has been an absolute fairy tale of a story throughout this year’s World Cup, so all projections, market values, and rankings go completely out the window. The Moroccans ascent to the semifinals has been the stuff of legend. They won Group F over Croatia, helped send No. 2 ranked Belgium home in the group stage by defeating them 2-nil, defeated Spain in penalty kicks in the Round of 16, and were in control of No. 9 Portugal in last Saturday’s quarterfinals with a 1-0 win. Morocco is the first country from the African continent to reach the semifinals. France, meanwhile, is exactly where they were expected to be. They dwarf Morocco’s market value of €241.10 million by nearly €700 million with Les Bleus’ roster being valued at €937 million. Kylian Mbappe is tied for the Golden Boot race with Lionel Messi with five goals, and France is coming off of a big 2-1 win over England to qualify for the semi-finals. So who are the players to watch? With France, their team is ripe from top-to-bottom. Attacker Antoine Griezmann and wingers Ousmane Dembélé and Mbappe, striker Olivier Giroud, midfielder Aurélien Tchouaméni, and keeper Hugo Lloris have all been in stellar form. Striker Youssef En-Nesyri is another player to watch after scoring the Morocco pulled off yet another stunning upset when defeating Portugal 1-0. Can they make more magic in Wednesday’s semifinal against France? eventual game-winner against Portugal, while fullback Achraf Hakimi is one of the best players in the world at his position. If the Moroccan’s can pull off another upset, it will likely be because of strong defense. If France has an Achilles heel, it will be their back line. France got lucky when Harry Kane missed his penalty kick late in the second half of the quarterfinals, a shot that would have forced overtime. Theo Hernandez looked bad barreling into England’s Mason Mount to create a penalty kick situation. Perhaps Morocco can target France’s back line with long balls to force a similar error. I’m going with a 2-1 France win; Morocco makes things interesting, but France’s powerful attack controls the action. No. 3 Argentina in the Final Can the Messi Magic keep going? Argentina entered the tournament as a favorite to win and have proven that playing ugly sometimes gets the job done. It hasn’t been a perfect display from the Argentines after nearly taking an exit in the group stage. Its 2-1 win over Australia in the Round of 16 was unconvincing, it went to penalty kicks with Netherlands after a 2-2 draw before prevailing 4-3 on PKs. Argentina versus France was a clear favorite to occur in the pre-tournament predictions. I had it penciled in as my guess until watching Argentina lose to Saudi Arabia to open the group stage. articles.text: Tap Dancing Christmas Trees perform this Sunday at exhibit Frequent visitors to Golden Gate Park will remember the Entwined installation, back at Peacock Meadow for the third year. New to this year’s art installation are live performances twice a week. The illuminate twice-a-week exhibit began in 2020 at the height of the COVID pandemic as a way to encourage people to come to Golden Gate Park. San Francisco artist Charles Gadeken created a whimsical, brightly lit wonderland where visitors can explore paths and sit under a grove of three entwined sculptural trees. Gadeken, an industrial artist, has worked in the creative field for over 25 years, and whose monumental interactive public artworks reimagine the world “post-nature.” His artwork commissions include Black Rock Arts Foundation, City of SF, Insomniac Events, Coachella, Absolut Vodka, City of Palo Alto, City of Calabasas, City of Los Altos, Stanford University, and more. Many of Charles’ works have been exhibited internationally. Entwined will remain in Golden Gate Park through March 2023 and remains illuminated until 10 p.m. each night. The project is sponsored by the San Francisco Parks Alliance. This Sunday, December 18, see the Tap Dancing Christmas Trees perform alongside the installation. For nearly three decades, the Oakland-based group of three dancers has performed at the Tree Lighting Ceremonies for San Francisco, Oakland, Hayward, Emeryville and Alameda under the direction of Pamm Drake. The Trees recently performed at the opening of the Piedmont Scout Christmas Tree Lot on November 26. The Trees will perform in Golden Gate Park on December 18 at 5 p.m. To learn more about the installation and its history, and the various performances now through March, visit https://sanfranciscoparksalliance.org/projects/ entwined/. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s current production of Matilda the Musical, based on the popular children’s book by Roald Dahl, will continue through December 23. Titular character Matilda is an extraordinary girl with a big imagination. Despite her unique and empathetic wit she is looked down upon by her family and wicked school headmistress Miss Trunchbull. Matilda’s closest confidante and friend is her sweet teacher Miss Honey, who fosters the little girl’s big personality. Gregory Lynch is cast as Miss Trunchbull; Mark Robinson and Mary Kalita play Matilda Wormwood’s wayward parents. Chanel Tilghman is Miss Honey. Performances are Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings. Tickets are available online at www.berkeleyplayhouse.org, or by calling (510) 845-8542, extension 351. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will introduce its first-ever sensory friendly performance of Nutcracker on Wednesday, December 21. The event is presented in collaboration with the San Francisco Bay Area Autism Society. Special accommodations have been made to the ballet for the December 21 performance that are friendly to those who experience sensory processing disorders, autism, post-traumatic stress disorder, and all neurodiverse audiences. It takes place in a relaxed and “shushfree” setting and is appropriate for all ages. Designated quiet areas will be available for guests. “As a musician, and parent of an autistic son, I’m especially sensitive to how much music and dance can touch the hearts of people with autism and special needs,” said Stephen Prutsman, President of Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area. “The holiday season can be stressful and isolating for autism and special needs families, so for a world-class company like San Francisco Ballet to open its doors and welcome our community is a landmark for the entire ballet world, and a tremendous gift for us.” This special version of Nutcracker is open to all audience members; but because it is adapted specifically to accommodate individuals with sensory sensitivities, guests are encouraged to familiarize themselves with the adjustments of the Sensory Friendly Performance. The performance begins at 7 p.m. Visit https://www.sfballet. org/nutcracker-sensory-friendly-performance/ to purchase tickets and to learn more about sensory friendly performances.
articles.title: SF Ballet introduces sensory friendly performance of Nutcracker on Dec. 21

articles.text: Sacha Grippando in talk at Center for the Arts this Saturday W i l l i a m S h a k e s p e a r e famously wrote “all that glitters is not gold”. This statement could not better sum up the Gilded Age, a period from 1870-1914 in America. This was a time of immense political, economic and social change and unrest. On the surface it was a time of glamor, innovation and immense wealth, the likes and scale of which had never been seen in the U,S. What better way to show one’s power than through the most dazzling jewelry ever made? Innovations in metalsmithing and lapidary coupled with the discovery of diamonds in South Africa heralded an era of jewelry made with superior craftsmanship and brilliance. Piedmont resident Sacha Grippando, a graduate gemologist from the Gemological Institute of America, is giving a free talk this coming Saturday, December 17, at Piedmont Center for the Arts at 5:00 p.m. Her lecture will focus on the history, the jewelry and some of the characters from this fascinating time period. It is the first in a series of planned lectures on jewelry. What better way to kick off the festive season than with a talk filled with glitter and sparkle? articles.text: Born Joseph Anthony Jacobi Passalaqua in 1929, Joe Pass grew up in Johnstown, Pennsylvania during the Depression. His father, Mariano, wanted to make sure his children didn’t follow his footsteps and work in the steel mill. Joe’s life in music started at age nine. Mariano could sense the budding talent and pushed Joe to practice many hours a day. Joe said later, “My father would go to the music store, and if he saw any book that said ‘guitar’ on it, he brought it home.” Joe learned scales and chord changes until they were second nature. “You have to have the instrument in your hand till it feels like an extension of yourself, and for me holding the guitar for seven hours a day, did just that,” he said. Joe recalled that when he was about 14 years old, his father would entertain friends, sitting around playing cards and ask Joe to play a song for them. He had to represent the whole song by himself, starting his development of chord solos. In his early teens, Joe performed with Gentlemen of Rhythm, a combo that played the music of guitarist Django Reinhardt. Other guitar influences involved in drugs”. Joe became an addict, and eventually served time in prison. When Joe moved to Los Angeles in 1960. he became a studio player and worked with Frank Sinatra, but still was an addict. Leonard Feather called him “the most exciting new talent on jazz guitar since Wes Montgomery.” Norman Granz signed Joe to Pablo records in 1973. Joe won a Grammy in ’74 for The Trio with Oscar Peterson. His Virtuoso album series of chord solos became popular. Joe performed with Bud Shank, George Shearing, Ray Brown, Niels-Henning Pedersen, Milt Jackson, Count Basie, Ella Fitzgerald, Benny Goodman and Duke Ellington. He remained active until his death in 1994 from cancer. The list appeared in the December 11 edition of the New York Times. “My favorite Young Adult thrillers are the ones that provide unexpected answers to big, terrifying questions about our world, our future and our fears. I love how they manage to electrify audiences while folding in beloved Y.A. tropes, like swoon-worthy high school romance, found family and, of course, young people forced to fix problems left to them by older generations,” wrote Abike-Iyimide. somewhere other than the West interest you, this book might just be your new favorite read. Her review is available at Nytimes.com/2022/12/11/books/ review/young-adult-thrillers. html. The Cousins by Karen M. McManus Though she’s known for her series One of Us Is Lying, my favorite novel from Karen M. McManus’s impressive catalog is her 2020 book, The Cousins. The novel is about three cousins who one summer are unexpectedly summoned to work for their wealthy but scornful grandmother, a matriarch who previously shunned her family. At the request of their parents, the cousins bend to their grandmother’s will for a chance to reclaim their inheritance and figure out what happened all those years ago that caused the rift in their family. Parts of this book rendered me speechless. This is a story steeped in generational secrets, filled with sharp and witty dialogue, and it features a unique and unforgettable twist. The Red Palace by June Hur Eighteenth-century Korea is the backdrop for this bloody historical thriller. The Red Palace follows a young nurse as she attempts to uncover the truth behind the murders of four women. Hur is known for her stunning female-centered historical Y.A. novels, and this is arguably her darkest book yet. It’s a story about the violence that society so often sweeps under the rug, but a closer look reveals many additional layers: “The Red Palace” is also about relationships — both distant and dear — and the family we choose. If slow-burn romances, well-paced plots and historical fiction set The Girls I’ve Been by Tess Sharpe The protagonist of The Girls I’ve Been, Nora, was raised by a con artist mother and brought up in a world of violence and deceit. It’s a life Nora has tried to escape, but when she finds herself in a bank robbery-hostage situation at the start of the book, she must tap into her past, and her index of false identities, to get everyone out of the situation alive. Y.A. often features strong female characters, and Nora is no different. While I loved Nora’s resilience, I admired even more the way Sharpe stressed the importance of giving survivors of all kinds of abuse the chance to love and be loved. Grown by Tiffany D. Jackson In this harrowing thriller, Tiffany D. Jackson manages to craft a story that is not only deeply heartfelt and relevant but also incredibly entertaining. The narrative follows Enchanted “Chanty” Jones, a 17-year-old aspiring musician whose dreams come true when she captures the interest of the musical superstar Korey Fields. Korey seems to be Enchanted’s ticket to stardom, but nothing is as it seems. The novel explores important topics, including the dark corners of the music industry, the adultification of Black girls and the consequences of abuses of power. This is a book that is filled to the brim with shocking twists and turns, but in “Grown,” Jackson also centers Black girls in conversations about abuse, discussions they are so often erased from. Death Note by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata This genre-bending manga offers readers an imaginative take on the Y.A. mystery thriller by showcasing an untraditional hero-villain dynamic. When 17-year-old Light Yagami gets hold of a notebook (the titular death note) that allows him to kill others by simply writing their names inside, he jumps at the chance, killing high-profile criminals in secret to rid the world of evil. Light begins to feel invincible until he finds himself under the scrutiny of the genius detective L. The story quickly becomes a game of cat and mouse, leaving readers at the edge of their seats anticipating whether or not Light will be caught. This story completely blew my mind and forever changed what I thought about thrillers as a genre. (I’d recommend Death Note for readers ages 14 and up — it sounds darker than it is, and it doesn’t get too graphic.) We Were Liars by E. Lockhart Before it became a BookTok obsession, We Were Liars was long a cult favorite in the Y.A. thriller space. I picked up this strangely structured yet beautifully written thriller shortly after it was published in 2014 and inhaled it in one sitting. The story follows the tortured mind of a teenage girl, Cady Sinclair, and the many secrets both she and her entire family harbor. I adored the unconventionality of this story, from the prose to the big revelations at the end. Lockhart’s lyrical thriller continues to enthrall readers years after its initial release, marking this novel as a future classic in the genre.

articles.text: The race to the end of the year is off with a big bang. Rain and storms and mountains of snow. Nature is making up for lost time. A big snafu in Piedmont gave us an embarrassment of riches over the weekend. And off we go… Publicists love the word “big”. Where would we be without it? That great promoter, Ed Sullivan, always gave us a “big show.” For the circus it was the big top. And for politicians it is the big picture. Perspective is everything. Local artist and lecturer Michael Stehr tells art lovers that shadow is a part of light. The big snafu in Piedmont resulted in two great concerts over the weekend. Berkeley Symphony presented its stellar brass ensemble in concert in the Community Center. They took the opportunity to appreciate the many wonderful things that Gray Cathrall has done for the community and for Berkeley Symphony in particular. At the very same time, the Diluvian String Quartet played a concert for an enthusiastic audience in the Piedmont Center for the arts. I learned long ago to appreciate events in small venues. The immortal violinist Jascha Heifetz actually preferred to play in small concert halls. I will never forget his numerous concerts in Hancock Auditorium at USC in Los Angeles. It was so much better to hear him up close rather than in the Hollywood Bowl. Festive holiday concerts are everywhere, and indeed ‘tis the season. There are sing-along Messiahs and balletic Nutcrackers everywhere. I hope that our Piedmont Chamber Orchestra will present a holiday concert. Some of my favorite presentations are the holiday concerts presented by Cantare con Vivo. The programs themselves are lots of fun, but there is a big side story to Cantare. Its music directors, David Morales and Julie Haydon, contribute mightily to the musical health of our area. They have established a musical organization which gives music lessons to some 3000 students in the East Bay. Some of these musical kids performed in the concert. Piedmont‘s favorite guitarist, Jaume Torrent, offered some philosophy on modern life. As he approaches his 70th birthday, he has been reevaluating all aspects of musical art. Torrent noted that the artists of the past probed the depths of music. Every artist of the past cultivated an individual personality. But at the same time they realized that “personality” must not defeat innate musical creativity. The composer and our musical art was all important. Jaume points out that commercialism has trampled those ideals of the past. We now have an acrobatic circus. Time marches on. At the same time we must keep in mind that music is a savior in all aspects. It is a unifying force which educates us in a way that anticipates a world liberated from stupidity, selfishness, and corruption. Catalonian classical guitarist and composer Jaume Torrent.

articles.text: The first time I tried a glass of sherry was when a friend handed me a glass of cold Fino style. Taken aback by the astringent taste, I replied “Whoa. That is bitter!” It is hard for me now to relate to that experience. 25 years later there is nothing that so perfectly marks the end of a workday and the beginning of a relaxing evening than a glass of frigid, dry, fino sherry. articles.text: It’s that time of the year when holiday shopping, gift giving and home decorating are top of mind. But maybe it’s time to take a step back and think about what and how we buy, wrap, give and decorate. Maybe there’s a better way that fills our holiday needs and at the same time, offers the biggest gift of all: helping save our climate, our environment, our future! Here are a few ideas: “Thrifting” Instead of ordering another new shirt, sweater, dress, or purse, check out local thrift shops where you can find clothing in excellent shape for bargain prices, as well as unique items that will find new life again and be treasured for years to come. Here’s a list of thrift store near us: https://www.piedmontconnect. org/thrifting. Reusable gift wrap Republic Services can recycle tissue paper but not coated, glossy or embellished wrapping paper or gift bags, plastic ribbons, bows or cellophane. Instead, save and reuse these items as well as gift boxes, for next year. Wrap presents in reusable gift wrap made of stretchable fabric, Kraft paper, or recycled wrapping paper. Get creative by wrapping presents in old maps or recruit children to draw magical pictures on recyclable paper bags or newspapers, and tie gifts with reusable fabric ribbons. Give experiences Instead of purchasing gift items, offer family and friends an enjoyable experience. Delight youngsters with a trip to the Oakland Zoo, Chabot Observatory, Academy of Sciences, Exploratorium, a ferry ride on the Bay, or any of dozens of Bay Area activities. Let children choose a non-profit organization to donate to in their name. Give the adults in your life tickets to a theater, concert or ballgame, dinner at a favorite restaurant, a local wine tasting venture, a museum exhibit. There are a plethora of diverse activities to select from in the Bay Area. Real vs. artificial trees Is it better to buy a real live Christmas tree every year or an artificial one that can be reused year after year? Studies have found that a real Christmas tree generates fewer environmental impacts than an artificial tree unless the artificial tree is reused for at least five years, at which point it has a smaller environmental impact than a real tree. Artificial trees are made from plastic and steel, take more energy to produce, many are shipped from China, and they cannot be recycled. Christmas tree farmers, on the other hand, replant a new tree for every one they harvest, and Republic Services collects and recycles them. Earth Friendly Tips also suggests a dozen ways to recycle or reuse your tree, yourself, from making coasters out of the wood and air fresheners from the pine needles to creating wildlife habitat from the entire tree. Or what about buying a living tree to plant in your yard? And there’s always the choice of creating your own artistic tree. However you decorate, be sure to use LED bulbs or solar powered lights in holiday lighting. It turns out there’s no need to be a Grinch by “going green” for the holidays. From buying second-hand to choosing sustainable products, there are plenty of ecofriendly ways to show your family, friends and the planet, lots of holiday love. Marjorie Blackwell is a Board Member of Piedmont Connect, a collaborative community organization supporting resident initiatives and city efforts to build a sustainable future. For more ideas on how to have an eco-friendly holiday, visit Piedmont Connect at https://www. piedmontconnect.org/eco-friendly-holidays.

articles.text: Have you ever had to throw away food that’s gone bad, even though you had every intention of eating it? According to a study published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics, the average U.S. household wastes 32% of its food. Wasted food is a major contributor to climate change. The production and transportation of food generates carbon emissions and when food is thrown into landfills, it generates methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Luckily, there are simple steps you can take to reduce your food waste at home, and in turn save money and lower your carbon footprint. The first step in reducing food waste is to buy only what you know you’ll eat. Next, choose the freshest produce. This means greens that aren’t wilted or yellowing at the edges, apples without brown spots, and potatoes that are firm. The freshest fruit will feel heavy for their size. If you have lots of produce in the fridge but aren’t sure what to make, try using the app Plant Jammer. It takes the ingredients you have and provides recipes that incorporate those ingredients. Storing food correctly can significantly impact its longevity. Many foods stay fresh for longer when stored outside the fridge. Tomatoes and bananas should be stored on the counter. Potatoes should be stored in a cool, dry, dark place in an open container for airflow. Onions and garlic don’t need to be kept from the light but should also be stored in a cool dry place with air flow. Other root vegetables, like carrots, parsnips, beets, turnips, and radishes, can last 3 weeks if stored in a crisper drawer on high humidity. Fresh herbs do well in a glass of water and greens are best stored unwashed in a zip-top bag. Additionally, cut carrots, celery, potatoes, and apples can be kept crisp when stored in cold water in the refrigerator. Even avocado halves can be kept fresh in water! To prolong freshness even more, change the water every few days. Fruits like apples, pears and bananas give off ethylene gas as they ripen, which in turn causes the produce around them to ripen faster. Lettuce, carrots, and broccoli will deteriorate rapidly if exposed to ethylene and should be stored away from apples. Lots of commonly disregarded food scraps are edible. Carrot, beet and radish greens are versatile and delicious. If you collect your veggie scraps and peels in the freezer, you can use them to make vegetable stock. Lettuce and green onions are particularly easy to grow from scraps. Even if you buy food with intention and store your produce perfectly, you’ll inevitably have some inedible food scraps. You can reduce your environmental impact by composting. Unlike when food decomposes in the landfill, compost does not produce methane. Putting your food scraps in the green bin is one of the easiest ways to lower your carbon footprint.

The group was pleased to have Doug Higashi with K-9 best friend Lucy, and Glen Tripp walk with them for the first time. Once again, the Walking on Wednesdays group had great weather for their weekly walk on December 7. The group has had good weather all year and December 7 was no exception. There was a near record turnout of 45 walkers and four K-9 best friends. Piedmont Recreation Department supervisor Eva Phalen told the group about classes available for older adults, including a line dancing class. Melba Yee will organize walks for the next several weeks in the absence of Dick Carter, with urban planner and architect Will Adams leading today’s walk, December 14. Melba Yee and Mike Henn will take the group down the hill to Zachary’s Pizza on Grand Avenue for a Holiday lunch on December 21. Part of the focus last week was on the history Sharon Avenue. A few years ago, Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi devoted almost an entire issue of the society’s publication to William E. Sharon, his family, and estate. The group decided it would walk to Sharon Avenue, discuss its history, and then continue on up to Sea View Avenue to see the Christmas decorations in some of the front yards. The walkers crossed Highland Avenue, went up Piedmont Court to a path that took them to Mountain Avenue, as its corner with Dormidera Avenue the Sharon history was shared. Born in 852, William Sharon grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872 he came to San Francisco, and went to Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, a successful banker and oner of a silver mine. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt there in 1876. He was elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. After the birth of the first three of their seven children but they wanted them to attend better schools and bought a home in Oakland in 1890. In 1893 the Sharons purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. In 1897 they hired Frederic Voorhess to design a home in Piedmont, a magnificent threestory house that they called Casa Montana. The Sharons with seven children, her mother, a housekeeper, cook, and gardener moved into Casa Montana in 1898. In 1914 the City of Piedmont, then 7 years old, imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property, and the Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically. In 1915 they subdivided their land into 20 lots in a development they called Sharon Terrace. The driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue, and the address changed from Mountain Avenue to 37 Sharon Avenue. Lots from the subdivision have frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues. William Sharon died at his home in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home with seven family members and two servants living there. Lillian Sharon continued to live in the mansion until 1934 when she moved to Oakland. Born in 852, William Sharon grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872 he came to San Francisco, and went to Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, a successful banker and oner of a silver mine. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt there in 1876. He was elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. After the birth of the first three of their seven children but they wanted them to attend better schools and bought a home in Oakland in 1890. In 1893 the Sharons purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. In 1897 they hired Frederic Voorhess to design a home in Piedmont, a magnificent threestory house that they called Casa Montana. The Sharons with seven children, her mother, a housekeeper, cook, and gardener moved into Casa Montana in 1898. In 1914 the City of Piedmont, then 7 years old, imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property, and the Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically. In 1915 they subdivided their land into 20 lots in a development they called Sharon Terrace. The driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue, and the address changed from Mountain Avenue to 37 Sharon Avenue. Lots from the subdivision have frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues. William Sharon died at his home in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home with seven family members and two servants living there.
